# 1. Introduction

The SIR model is a compartmental model used to describe
how an infectious disease spreads through a population.

It has three compartments:

- S = Susceptible
- I = Infectious
- R = Recovered

The direction of movement is:

S -> I -> R

# 2. Load the required package

```{r}
# Install deSolve once if it is not already installed.
# install.packages("deSolve")

# Load the package used to solve differential equations.
library(deSolve)
```


# 3. Define the initial population

```{r}
# Total starting population
initP <- 100

# Initially infectious people
initI <- 1

# Initially recovered people
initR <- 0

# Everyone else is susceptible.
initS <- initP - initI - initR

# Store the initial values in a named vector.
istate <- c(
  S = initS,
  I = initI,
  R = initR
)

# Display the initial conditions.
istate
```

# 4. Define the model parameters

```{r}
# Natural birth and death rate per day.
# 50 years are converted into days:
# 50 years x 52 weeks x 7 days = 18,200 days.
mu <- 1 / (50 * 52 * 7)

# Transmission parameter per day.
beta <- 0.4

# Recovery rate per day.
# The reciprocal gives a mean infectious period of 10 days.
tau <- 1 / 10

# Combine parameters into one named vector.
parameters <- c(
  mu = mu,
  beta = beta,
  tau = tau
)

# Display the parameters.
parameters
```


# 5. Understand the SIR equations

The total population is:

P = S + I + R


The force of infection is:

lambda = beta * I / P

The differential equations are:

dS/dt = mu*P - mu*S - lambda*S

dI/dt = lambda*S - tau*I - mu*I

dR/dt = tau*I - mu*R

# 6. Write the SIR model function

```{r}
# Define a function containing the three SIR equations.
# deSolve will use this function to calculate changes over time.

SIR_model <- function(t, state, parameters) {

  # Make the state variables and parameters available by their names.
  with(as.list(c(state, parameters)), {

    # Calculate the total population.
    P <- S + I + R

    # Calculate the force of infection.
    # This is the infection pressure experienced by a susceptible person.
    lambda <- beta * I / P

    # Change in susceptible population.
    # Births add people; natural deaths and infection remove people.
    dS <- mu * P - mu * S - lambda * S

    # Change in infectious population.
    # New infections add people; recovery and natural deaths remove people.
    dI <- lambda * S - tau * I - mu * I

    # Change in recovered population.
    # Recovery adds people; natural deaths remove people.
    dR <- tau * I - mu * R

    # Return the three rates of change.
    # The order must match the initial state vector:
    # S, I, R.
    list(c(dS, dI, dR))
  })
}
```

# 7. Choose the simulation time

```{r}
# Start simulation at day 0.
time_start <- 0

# End simulation at day 365.
time_stop <- 365

# Request output every 0.1 day.
deltat <- 0.1

# Create a sequence of time points.
tps <- seq(
  time_start,
  time_stop,
  by = deltat
)

# Check the first few time points.
head(tps)
```

# 8. Solve the differential equations

```{r}
# Use the ode() function from deSolve.
# y = initial compartment values.
# times = requested output times.
# func = our SIR model function.
# parms = model parameters.

out <- deSolve::ode(
  y = istate,
  times = tps,
  func = SIR_model,
  parms = parameters
)

# Convert the output into a data frame.
out <- as.data.frame(out)

# View the first few results.
head(out)

# Check the output column names.
colnames(out)
```

# 9. Plot infectious people over time

```{r}
# Plot time on the horizontal axis
# and infectious people on the vertical axis.

plot(
  out$time,
  out$I,
  type = "l",
  col = "red",
  lwd = 2,
  xlab = "Time (days)",
  ylab = "Number of infectious people",
  main = "SIR Model: Infectious Population Over Time"
)
```

# 10. Plot all three compartments

```{r}
# Plot susceptible people.
plot(
  out$time,
  out$S,
  type = "l",
  col = "blue",
  lwd = 2,
  ylim = range(out[, c("S", "I", "R")]),
  xlab = "Time (days)",
  ylab = "Number of people",
  main = "SIR Model: All Compartments"
)

# Add infectious people.
lines(
  out$time,
  out$I,
  col = "red",
  lwd = 2
)

# Add recovered people.
lines(
  out$time,
  out$R,
  col = "darkgreen",
  lwd = 2
)

# Add a legend to identify each line.
legend(
  "right",
  legend = c("Susceptible", "Infectious", "Recovered"),
  col = c("blue", "red", "darkgreen"),
  lty = 1,
  lwd = 2
)
```

# 11. Check whether the population is conserved

```{r}
# Add the three compartments at every time point.
out$total_population <- out$S + out$I + out$R

# View the first few totals.
head(out$total_population)

# Find the smallest and largest total population.
range(out$total_population)
```

In this model, births and natural deaths balance,
so the total population should remain approximately 100.

# 12. Calculate the basic reproduction number

```{r}
# Basic reproduction number at the disease-free
# equilibrium, when everyone is susceptible.

R0 <- beta / (tau + mu)

# Display the result.
R0
```

Interpretation:

R0 estimates the average number of secondary infections
caused by one infectious person in a fully susceptible
population, under the model assumptions.

# 13. Experiment: increase transmission

```{r}
# Make a separate copy of the original parameters.
high_beta_parameters <- parameters

# Increase beta fivefold.
high_beta_parameters["beta"] <-
  5 * parameters["beta"]

# Solve the model using the higher transmission rate.
out_high_beta <- deSolve::ode(
  y = istate,
  times = tps,
  func = SIR_model,
  parms = high_beta_parameters
)

out_high_beta <- as.data.frame(out_high_beta)

# Compare the infectious population with the baseline.
plot(
  out$time,
  out$I,
  type = "l",
  col = "blue",
  lwd = 2,
  xlab = "Time (days)",
  ylab = "Infectious people",
  main = "Effect of Increasing Transmission"
)

lines(
  out_high_beta$time,
  out_high_beta$I,
  col = "red",
  lwd = 2
)

legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c("Baseline beta", "Higher beta"),
  col = c("blue", "red"),
  lty = 1,
  lwd = 2
)
```

# 14. Experiment: decrease transmission

```{r}
# Create another independent copy of baseline parameters.
low_beta_parameters <- parameters

# Reduce beta to half its baseline value.
low_beta_parameters["beta"] <-
  0.5 * parameters["beta"]

# Solve the model.
out_low_beta <- deSolve::ode(
  y = istate,
  times = tps,
  func = SIR_model,
  parms = low_beta_parameters
)

out_low_beta <- as.data.frame(out_low_beta)

# Compare the infectious curves.
plot(
  out$time,
  out$I,
  type = "l",
  col = "blue",
  lwd = 2,
  xlab = "Time (days)",
  ylab = "Infectious people",
  main = "Effect of Decreasing Transmission"
)

lines(
  out_low_beta$time,
  out_low_beta$I,
  col = "green3",
  lwd = 2
)

legend(
  "topright",
  legend = c("Baseline beta", "Lower beta"),
  col = c("blue", "green3"),
  lty = 1,
  lwd = 2
)
```

# 15. Inspect the model results

```{r}
# Find the maximum number of infectious people.
peak_infections <- max(out$I)

# Find the time when infections reach their maximum.
peak_time <- out$time[which.max(out$I)]

# Display both results.
peak_infections
peak_time

# Check for negative compartment values.
min(out$S)
min(out$I)
min(out$R)
```

# 16. Important interpretation points

- S decreases as susceptible people become infected.
- I increases when new infections exceed recoveries and deaths.
- I decreases when recoveries and deaths exceed new infections.
- R increases through recovery and decreases through natural deaths.
- Increasing beta generally increases transmission.
- The total population remains approximately constant
  because births balance natural deaths in this model.
